title: Evidence
subtitle: New Orleans, New York and Washington, D.C.
focus: The family-reunion festival (1990s R&B, new jack swing, neo-soul, a gospel Sunday), the long line from spirituals to swing on the concert-hall stage, and the national stage and who gets honoured

intro.t: New Orleans, the first Saturday in December. Twenty-eight days to Watch Night.
The van is waiting outside the train station, right where the Whitewall Ladies left it. A fresh pinstripe down both sides. MT. NEBO YOUTH CHOIR, untouched.
Note on the dash. 'Didn't touch the letters. - W.'
Look at the Choir. Two thousand miles and not one scratch. Somebody's mother did not get a phone call this week.
The train from New York comes in forty minutes late, which Nana Dess will later describe as 'on time, for a train'.
She steps down in her red usher jacket, brass buttons done to the neck, one small suitcase, and looks the four of you over the way she looks over a line around the block.
Hm. Tuesday. Gloves in your pocket, baby? Good. Come here.
Then Ruth, who has ridden in the front seat since Memphis and defended it against all comers, gets out and holds the passenger door open.
Front seat's yours, Dess. I kept it warm since Memphis.
Sixty years, and the first thing said between them is about a seat. Fine. Every reunion starts with somebody sitting down.

outro.t: North in the dark, out of Washington. The heater ticks. Thirteen days to Watch Night, and in the van, nobody talks.
Ruth is asleep with her hat over her face. The Professor is pretending to be. Ren has his bass across her knees. Deacon taps two and four on the window glass.
Five names on a list at the staff door of Midtown Arena. Tuesday has read the letter four times looking for a page forty-one. There isn't one.
She puts on her glasses, takes out her phone and starts at the top of her contacts.
Gloria? Odessa Fontaine. Fine, baby, fine. Listen. You still working Midtown? How many red jackets you got in that locker room?
Mm-hm. Five. Long ones. One for a tall man with a cane, and he will complain about the sleeves.
She trained half the ushers in this city. She has every one of their numbers. By the New Jersey line she has called eleven of them.
I know that voice. That's the one that hollers.

gigs.title: Family Reunion
gigs.blurb: A festival night that feels like a family reunion. Backstage, five people share a room for the first time since 1967.

vibe.label: 1990s R&B, new jack swing and neo-soul

challenge.text: Family reunion: play this set with at least 2 people.

before.t: Out front, forty thousand people, half of them in matching family-reunion T-shirts. Backstage, exactly one room with a door that shuts: six folding chairs, a box fan, and a plate of pralines nobody has touched.

Ruth in her church hat. Deacon, who said no in Houston and came anyway in Marcus's slab. Ren, with his bass on her back. The Professor, off his first flight home in fifty-seven years. And Dess, still in the red jacket from the train.
Deacon. Low. Sister. Professor. Dess. Sixty years I have waited to hear those five in one room, and so far the loudest thing in it is the fan.
Well. Who got fat?
Deacon laughs first. Then Ren, then Dess behind her hand, then the Professor, last and entirely against his will.
Odessa. I rehearsed this for eleven hours on an airplane. We were grown. We signed our own names. You were nineteen and he was fifty.
That is not a trade. That is a robbery with a pen.
Nobody moves. The box fan turns its head, as if it wants to hear what comes next.
...Dess.
He has not called her that since 1969. It lands right on the one. I would know.
Sit down, Aurelius. You flew a long way to stand up.
Daddy wrote 'D. got paper.' He never wrote anything worse than that. For him that's forgiving.
Then this goes home. One pocket ledger, returned to its owner. I know. Not with his name on something.
Yet.
We're on. Don't go anywhere.
Pocket, I'm eighty-four. Anywhere is a long way.

afterWin.t: By the second song the T-shirts were on their feet. One family held their grandmother up on a folding chair so she could see. She waved at the wings like she knew somebody back there.
After, in the room with the door: the notice the Counselor sent ahead. One page. Five lines for five signatures. A pen Tuesday has wiped clean with a glove.
Deacon signs slow, the way he counts in. Ruth signs with a flourish and dots the i twice, to be sure.
The last thing I signed in this country was a release for fifteen dollars and a plate. I have read this one twice.
Lemuel Castile. By his left hand's daughter.
Nana. Your turn.
I haven't signed that name on anything but a timecard since 1967.
She signs it anyway. Odessa Fontaine, all the way across the line. No initial. No abbreviation.
There. Now it's got his name on something.
Fun fact - the last time all five of these names were on one sheet of paper -
'Tuesday. Not now.' Five voices, one downbeat. Deacon counted it in without meaning to.
...Okay. That was beautiful. I'm writing that down.

afterLose.t: Reunions run long. Nobody's leaving. Again.
I'm sixty years late to this party already. One more set won't hurt. Run it back.

gigs.title: Evidence: A Concert in Five Exhibits
gigs.blurb: The Counselor has booked a concert hall for a deposition you can dance to. One exhibit before every song.

challenge.text: Entered into the record: earn a gold star on one song.

before.t: New York, the middle of December. The Uptown Concert Hall: red plush, gold boxes, and a ceiling built so a whisper on the stage reaches the top balcony. Outside, the poster says EVIDENCE: A CONCERT IN FIVE EXHIBITS.
Onstage, a lectern. Beside it, a table with a white cloth like a church supper, and the Evidence Box. Beside that, Tuesday, in a black dress and white cotton gloves, standing very straight.
Good evening. My name is Ngozi Pryce, and tonight is a deposition you can dance to.
Your tickets were twenty dollars. My opening statement is included. Cross-examination is extra.
Exhibit A. One reel box.
That was Low's pen.
Exhibit B. One pocket ledger. Fifteen dollars and a plate.
That's his.
Exhibit C. One hymnal page.

In the front row Ruth mouths the number. Two eleven. Beside her, Deacon has started tapping two and four on the armrest, and the man in the next seat, who paid twenty dollars, has started doing it too.
Exhibit D. One snare head.
Exhibit E. One chart. The paper Gus Lark didn't write.
Entered without a number: the dead wax. There are ten million copies in this city's basements. Go home and look.
Ready when the court is.
Band, you may proceed.

afterWin.t: Five exhibits, five songs. After the closer the applause started in the top balcony and came down through the gold boxes like weather.
At the lectern, the Counselor takes out her phone, types for exactly as long as the applause lasts, and presses one button.
Filed. Now they have to answer.
That's it? Sixty years, and it's a button?
Most of the law is a button. The sixty years are the hard part. That was forty dollars, and worth it.
At the stage door, Bryce Whitlock is waiting with a folder, the way other men wait with flowers.
Mrs. Fontaine. With Ms. Lark's compliments. Lantern's national gala, in Washington, honouring Augustus Lark as composer.
Everybody watches her hands. Tuesday takes one careful step back, out of range.
Odessa does not tear it. She reads it twice, folds it once, and buttons it into the pocket of her red jacket.
Dess? You ain't gonna...?
No, baby. They invited me. I'm going to show up.

afterLose.t: The court will take a short recess. That means: again.
Objection noted. Overruled by me. Run it back.

gigs.title: The Gala
gigs.blurb: A national gala honouring Augustus Lark as composer. The room claps on one and three. Play it right anyway.

challenge.text: Keep two and four in a room that claps on one and three: five stars on every song.

before.t: Washington, a week before Christmas. The Capital Arts Center: marble, a red carpet, a string quartet in the lobby, and a banner forty feet tall. AUGUSTUS LARK, COMPOSER.
Five hundred people in black tie. Before the night is out, every one of them will clap on one and three. I can tell by the shoes.
A quiet room off the main hall. Leather chairs, Gus Lark in oils over the mantel, and tea. There is always tea.
Thank you all for coming. Mrs. Fontaine. Mr. Arceneaux. Miss Pettis. Professor Finch. Ms. Castile. The house would like to settle this tonight, quietly, and well.
A payment to each of you and to your families. A plaque in every Lantern school. And on every copy from now on, your names, under the word 'performers'. If the filing is withdrawn.
Performers. Not authors. That one word is worth more than the cheque, and everyone in this room knows it. I noticed that for free.
If it helps with the timing: the claimants are in their eighties. Perpetua is patient.
There is a time to keep and a time to cast away, Mrs. Fontaine. I am only asking which this is.
Ellery looks at his tablet. Odessa says nothing at all. She lets the silence sit in the leather chair beside her until it is the loudest thing in the room.
Miss Lark. We don't want your building. We want our names on the door.
The tribute. A film of Gus Lark in a dinner jacket, cutting a ribbon. Applause. Then, before the medal, Kingston Lark walks to the podium. He is not on the program.
I was asked to say a few words about my great-grandfather. I rehearsed them for a month. I'm not going to say them.
I'm asking that this honour be held until the record is corrected. That's all. Thank you.
Five hundred people do not know what to do with that. So they clap. On one and three.
Hm. That boy just stopped rehearsing.
Then so do we. We're on.

afterWin.t: Two and four, three songs straight, in a room that wanted one and three. By the closer the back rows had come over to your side. The front rows never did. The front rows paid more.
A service corridor behind the hall. Coat racks, a fire door, folding tables. Vivienne Lark is alone in it, and then she isn't.
Walk with me. No folders, no lawyers. I would like one conversation in this matter that nobody is billing for.
I was twelve. Grandfather's house, Christmas week. I was on the stairs, where I was not supposed to be, and he was on the telephone with a man from Detroit.
'Son, there is no paper with your name on it.' Then he hung up, and came and asked me what I wanted for Christmas.
When I took the house I found his file, with her contract in it. That is why my first letter went to your grandmother. I knew exactly whose door I was knocking on.
I have spent thirty years being the best steward a stolen thing ever had.
Why tell me?
Because on Watch Night you will be standing nearer the microphone than anyone. Someone near it ought to know.
Ms. Lark. Security has the list for Midtown. The claimants are not to be admitted. The opening act, however...
Is under contract, Mr. Whitlock. The Opening Act may not be removed from any date it shows up for. My clients intend to show up.
Page forty-one. Nobody ever reads the last page. Ask five musicians in 1967.

afterLose.t: Rooms like this clap wrong on purpose, baby. Don't let them move you. Again.
One and three. Honestly. Run it back, and keep your own time.

afterChallenge.t: 12:58 a.m., Watch Night, 1967. The control room at Lantern. One desk lamp, the party still going upstairs, and a sheet of paper on the desk.
Gus's release was one page long. It came down to three promises: no credit, no claim, no talk.
Each of them got fifteen dollars and a plate from the party upstairs: fried chicken, greens, a slice of sweet potato pie. Ruth said grace over hers. Deacon ate standing up.
Deacon signed. Ruth signed. The Professor signed and blotted it, which nobody else bothered to do. Low signed last.
Then Low opened his little book on his knee and wrote: '$15 + plate.'
At the other end of the desk, Dess signed a different paper. Longer. Nobody counted out fifteen dollars for her.
Low saw. He did not say one word. He wrote a second line under the first, smaller: 'D. got paper. We got a plate.'
Behind the glass, while they ate, Gus dubbed the four bars onto a fresh reel for the pressing plant in Philadelphia. He started the copy at the downbeat.
No talkback. No roll call. No laugh. Just me, eleven seconds, already on my way to being somebody else's.
